title: Perceived borrowing costs are converting household financing decisions into forgone purchases, cheaper substitutes, and unequal flexibility
source_unit: Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia Consumer Finance Institute, Are Household Perceptions of Borrowing Costs Creating Spending Headwinds?
geography: United States; nationally representative survey of adults fielded July 20-23, 2026

denominator.unit: survey respondents with complete observations in the borrowing-cost analysis; nationally representative adult survey just over 4,000

forgone_large_purchase.unit: percent reporting considering borrowing for a large purchase but deciding not to make it for financial reasons in the prior six months

high_financing_cost_reason.unit: percent of those forgoing a purchase citing financing cost as the primary reason

all_respondents_high_cost_forgone.unit: percent of all respondents who chose not to make a large purchase because borrowing costs were too high

price_reason.unit: percent of those forgoing a purchase citing the item price as the primary reason

saving_reason.unit: percent of those forgoing a purchase saying saving or investing offered better value

borrowing_cost_conversion.value: Credit conditions are becoming a direct consumption constraint, not only a background financial variable

observations.method: Consumer Finance Institute survey fielded July 20-23, 2026 with a nationally representative sample of just over 4,000 adults; report uses descriptive tables and regression analysis.
observations.uncertainty: The outcome is self-reported forgone or altered purchase behavior, not transaction data; the report identifies associations and stated reasons rather than a fully causal estimate of interest-rate effects.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults considering large purchases such as homes, cars, or appliances, with income, age, family composition, employment, homeownership, debt, and asset differences analyzed.
observations.counterinterpretation: Some forgone purchases may reflect prudent saving, item-price concerns, or better alternatives rather than harmful credit exclusion; delaying a purchase can be adaptive or costly depending on necessity.

observations.period: July 2026; perceived affordability and financial decision salience

denominator.unit: respondents in the interest-rate importance and affordability table

rates_important.unit: percent rating interest rates extremely or very important in financing a large purchase

rates_top_two.unit: percent ranking interest rates among the top two purchase-financing factors

rates_unaffordable_typical_borrower.unit: percent agreeing current interest rates make most loans unaffordable to the typical borrower

item_price_top_factor.unit: percent ranking item price as the most important financing-decision component

affordability_perception.value: Consumers evaluate financing through both the loan rate and the price of the item, with perceived unaffordability shaping whether a purchase remains actionable

observations.method: Survey questions comparing interest rate, item price, monthly payment, and loan length, with a general question about affordability for typical borrowers.
observations.uncertainty: The typical-borrower framing is not a respondent-specific affordability measure; stated importance does not establish actual credit access or repayment burden.
observations.subgroup: U.S. consumers across income ranges and demographic groups, including those with different debt and asset positions.
observations.counterinterpretation: Consumers may report rates as important because they are salient in public discussion, while actual decisions may be driven by income, item price, monthly payment, or necessity.

observations.period: July 2026; income, debt, and asset-conditioned flexibility

denominator.unit: respondents in the interest-rate analysis; subgroup estimates are descriptive/regression-based

income_stability_forgone.value: The share reporting forgone financing was relatively stable across income ranges, with the highest-income group only five percentage points below the lowest-income group

personal_loan_association.unit: percentage-point association between personal-loan holding and likelihood of forgoing financing relative to reference conditions in the report's regression

credit_card_association.unit: percentage-point association between credit-card holding and likelihood of forgoing financing relative to reference conditions

investment_buffer.value: Consumers with potentially higher-return investments were less likely to cite high borrowing costs as the reason for forgoing financing and more likely to cite investment value

unequal_flexibility.value: Borrowing and asset positions shape whether households experience rates as binding, even when headline forgone-purchase shares look similar across income groups

observations.method: Regression analysis controlling for income, unemployment, age, education, race, family composition, homeownership, debt, and assets; report cautions that results are associations.
observations.uncertainty: The reported coefficients do not prove that debt or assets cause forgoing; unobserved liquidity, credit scores, purchase needs, and financial sophistication may influence both debt position and decisions.
observations.subgroup: Households differentiated by income, debt composition, investment holdings, age, family composition, employment, education, race, and homeownership.
observations.counterinterpretation: Personal-loan holders may be seeking financing for inherently larger or more urgent purchases; investments may proxy for broader financial capacity rather than create a direct buffer.

observations.period: July 2026; cheaper substitution and information framing

denominator.unit: main survey respondents for financing-attitude analysis; follow-up framing experiment N=1,417

cheaper_alternative_purchase.unit: percent of respondents choosing an alternative less-expensive purchase primarily because of financing cost

lender_cost_priming_control.unit: percent of control group selecting the lowest affordable-rate category

lender_cost_priming_treatment.unit: percent of treatment group selecting the lowest affordable-rate category after lender costs were referenced

affordable_rate_treatment.unit: percent; average lower-bound rate selected by treatment group

affordable_rate_control.unit: percent; average lower-bound rate selected by control group

framing_route.value: Information about lenders' costs changed perceived affordability thresholds in the survey experiment

observations.method: Main survey plus randomized follow-up survey conducted July 29-30, 2026, varying whether the affordable-rate question referenced lenders' cost of funds.
observations.uncertainty: The framing effect is observed in a survey response, not a market transaction; it does not establish durable financial-literacy change or actual borrowing behavior.
observations.subgroup: U.S. consumers with varying awareness of current rates, debt, assets, and financial experience.
observations.counterinterpretation: The wording may have changed interpretation of the question rather than beliefs about real affordability; a lower stated threshold can coexist with continued borrowing for necessary purchases.

related_sources.claim: Philadelphia Fed LIFE Survey context and quarterly consumer-finance data series.

boundary: This record adds a consumer-credit conversion layer: perceived borrowing costs move households from intended purchases toward forgone purchases, cheaper substitutes, saving/investment, or changed affordability thresholds, with debt and asset positions shaping flexibility. It does not establish actual transactions, causal interest-rate effects, credit denial, long-run welfare, or universal income gradients.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official Philadelphia Fed report page and PDF reviewed for survey field dates, sample, forgone purchases, reasons, income/debt/asset associations, cheaper substitution, and randomized framing experiment.
